title: How to Actually Prepare for a Winter Ski Holiday (From People Who Live It)
excerpt: Forget the generic packing lists. Here's what seasoned skiers and locals actually do in the weeks before a ski trip — and what most first-timers miss.

seo.title: How to Prepare for a Ski Holiday | SkiBooker Insider Guide
seo.description: A local instructor's no-nonsense guide to preparing for your winter ski holiday — fitness, gear, lessons, and the small things most people forget.

children.text: There's a moment, usually about three days into a ski holiday, when you realise you should have started preparing weeks ago. Your legs are burning, your goggles fog up every run, and the lesson you booked turns out to be the wrong level. Sound familiar?

We've spent enough winters watching guests arrive in resort to know the patterns. The people who have the best week aren't necessarily the strongest skiers — they're the ones who prepared properly. Here's what actually matters.
Get your legs in before you arrive

Skiing punishes the unprepared quadriceps like nothing else. Six weeks out, start doing wall-sits. Three sets of 45 seconds, three times a week. Add lunges and step-ups. If you do nothing else, do this.

The reason isn't just comfort — tired legs cause most ski injuries. By day three of a holiday, fatigue compounds, technique falls apart, and that's when knees go. A bit of conditioning before you arrive means you ski better, longer, and safer.
Book your lessons before you book your accommodation

This sounds backwards, but hear us out. Good instructors in popular resorts get booked solid by October for peak weeks. By the time you've sorted flights and chalets in November, you're left with whoever's available — which often isn't the right fit.
Lock in lessons first, especially if you have specific needs (kids, mixed-ability groups, off-piste guiding). Then build the rest of the trip around them.
The gear conversation nobody has

Renting in resort is fine. But there's a hierarchy: boots matter most, then skis, then poles (which barely matter at all). If you're going to splurge on one thing, get properly fitted boots — either bought at home or pre-booked at a quality resort fitter rather than the queue-on-arrival rental shop.
For clothing, the unsexy truth is that mid-layers and socks make more difference than your jacket. One good merino base layer and decent ski socks will transform your week.
Sort the boring admin early

EHIC or GHIC card (if you're a UK or EU traveller), travel insurance that explicitly covers winter sports off-piste if relevant, lift pass pre-booking (often 10-15% cheaper than gate prices), and airport transfers. Resort transfers in particular sell out for Saturday changeovers — book them when you book your flights.
The week before: small things that matter

Break in new boots by wearing them around the house for 30 minutes a day. Charge your action camera batteries. Download offline maps of the resort to your phone. Pack ibuprofen, blister plasters, and lip balm with SPF — the three things you'll definitely need and definitely forget.
And finally: arrive a day early if you possibly can. The difference between starting your first ski day jet-lagged versus rested is enormous. You'll ski better, learn faster, and enjoy it more.
The best ski holidays aren't about luck or expensive kit. They're about the unglamorous preparation that happens in October and November. Get those right, and the rest takes care of itself.

title: Top Tips for Skiing with the Family (From Instructors Who See It All)
excerpt: Family ski holidays can be magical or miserable, and the difference usually comes down to a few small decisions. Here's what we've learned from teaching thousands of families.

seo.title: Family Skiing Tips | Expert Advice for Ski Holidays with Kids
seo.description: Practical, hard-won advice for family ski holidays — from picking the right resort to managing meltdowns on the chairlift. Written by working ski instructors.

children.text: We've taught a lot of families. The honeymooning couples come and go, the gap-year crews blur together, but families — families we remember. Mostly because family ski holidays sit on a knife edge between magical week and unmitigated disaster, and the difference often comes down to a handful of decisions made before you even arrive.
Here's what actually works.
Pick the resort for the weakest skier, not the strongest
This is the single most common mistake. Dad wants Verbier, so the family goes to Verbier, and then the seven-year-old spends a week crying on a red run that's too steep while mum tries to keep up.

Choose a resort with genuinely excellent beginner terrain — wide blues, gentle greens, dedicated learner areas separate from the through-traffic. Strong skiers in the family will find more than enough to keep them entertained. Beginners in resorts designed for advanced skiers will not.
Don't try to teach your own kids

We say this as parents and as instructors: it ends in tears, usually both yours and theirs. Children listen to instructors in ways they will never listen to their parents. Book proper lessons, drop them off, ski yourselves, come back at lunch. Everyone is happier.

For kids under six, look for instructors who specialise in teaching young children — it's a completely different skill from teaching adults. And consider whether group or private suits your child. Sociable confident kids thrive in groups. Anxious or younger children often do far better one-to-one.
The lunch problem is the real problem

Adults can ski through lunch. Children cannot. Plan your day around a proper, sit-down lunch with actual food — not a snack on the chairlift. Energy crashes in cold kids happen fast, and once they've crashed, the afternoon is over.

Many families find a half-day ski morning, lunch, and a short afternoon works far better than trying to push through. The kids ski more total minutes because they're not exhausted, and nobody ends up in tears at 3pm.
Layers, not big coats

Children overheat fast going up, then freeze fast standing in lift queues. The solution is layers — multiple thin layers they can add and remove — rather than one giant puffer jacket. Always pack a spare pair of gloves in your backpack. Wet gloves are the fastest route to a child wanting to go home.
Build in a non-ski day

A six-day ski holiday with kids is too much. Plan one day off — go swimming, find an ice rink, visit a husky park, do anything that isn't skiing. Kids come back to the slopes on day five fresh and keen rather than dragging.
Manage expectations, including your own

You're not going to ski the way you did pre-kids. You're going to ski less, ski slower, and ski easier terrain. That's not a bad holiday — it's a different holiday. The parents who accept this have a great time. The ones who fight it spend the week frustrated.

The best family ski holidays we see aren't the ones at the fanciest resorts with the priciest chalets. They're the ones where the parents made smart choices upfront, lowered the right expectations, and let the kids actually enjoy themselves. Get those right, and you'll be back next year.

title: The Best Things to Do in Morzine (Beyond the Obvious Pistes)
excerpt: A local's guide to Morzine — the runs worth your time, the restaurants worth the detour, and the things most guidebooks miss entirely.

seo.title: Best Things to Do in Morzine | Local Insider Guide 2026
seo.description: What to do in Morzine according to people who actually ski there — best pistes, top restaurants, après favourites, and off-mountain activities worth your time.

children.text: Morzine has a reputation as the British-friendly gateway to the Portes du Soleil, and that's mostly fair. What that reputation undersells is how genuinely good the skiing is, how much character the town has retained, and how easy it is to spend a week here without ever doing the same run twice.
Here's what we'd actually do with a week in Morzine.
Ski the Portes du Soleil properly

The Portes du Soleil is 600+ kilometres of linked pistes across 12 resorts straddling the French-Swiss border. Most visitors stay on the Morzine-Les Gets side, which is excellent — but you're missing the point if you don't venture further.

Head over to Avoriaz on a sunny morning (the village is car-free and feels like another planet), then drop down into Châtel for lunch. The classic Swiss-side day is the route via Les Crosets to Champéry — quieter pistes, dramatic scenery, and the chance to say you skied to Switzerland for lunch.
For something different, the Hauts Forts black runs above Avoriaz are some of the most underrated descents in France. Steep, long, and almost always empty on weekdays.
The lunch spots locals actually use
Skip the obvious on-piste self-services.
Chez Nannon
above Les Lindarets is the genuine article — a tiny mountain restaurant doing proper Savoyard food.
La Cremaillère
at the top of the Pleney lift is reliably good and has the views. For something simple and brilliant,
Le Plan des Lacs
does a tartiflette that has ruined every other tartiflette for us.
In town,
L'Atelier
does serious modern French food in an unfussy setting.
La Chamade
is the splash-out dinner. And if you want a quiet local spot,
La Grange
does fondue the way it's meant to be done.
Après that isn't a meat market
Morzine has a deserved reputation for late nights, but it's also possible to have a civilised drink. The
Cavern
is the loud option (and good fun if that's what you want).
Le Tremplin
by the main lift is the genuine après spot — outdoor terrace, live music most afternoons, locals and visitors mixed.
For something quieter,
Bec Jaune
is a brewery doing properly good craft beer. Worth a stop even if you're not staying for the night.
When you don't want to ski
The natural hot springs at
Les Bains de Morzine
are a perfect rest-day stop — outdoor pools surrounded by snow, exactly what tired legs need.
The
husky sledding
at Plateau de Loex is touristy but legitimately fun. Book ahead.
For non-skiing companions or kids, the
Indiana'Ventures
snowshoe tours run guided routes through quieter forest trails — good way to see the landscape without lift passes.
And if you've got a car,
Annecy
is an hour away. The lake town in winter is gorgeous and worth a day if the weather turns.
The thing nobody tells you

Morzine sits at a relatively low altitude (1000m), which means in poor snow years the village runs can be patchy. The lifts to Avoriaz (1800m) are reliable — just don't expect to ski back to your front door in March. Build that into your planning and you won't be disappointed.
Morzine rewards people who explore. Stay too close to the centre and you'll have a fine holiday. Push out into the wider Portes du Soleil and you'll have a great one.

title: The Best Things to Do in Méribel (A Local Instructor's Guide)
excerpt: Méribel sits at the heart of the world's largest ski area, but the best of it isn't always obvious. Here's what we'd actually do with a week there.

seo.title: Best Things to Do in Méribel | Insider Guide to the Three Valleys
seo.description: What to do in Méribel — the pistes worth your time, the lunches worth the detour, and the activities locals actually recommend. A working instructor's guide.

children.text: Méribel has a slightly awkward reputation: too British, too expensive, too in-the-middle. None of those are quite fair. What Méribel actually is, is the natural centre of the largest linked ski area on the planet, and a village that — for all its development — has held on to its wooden-chalet charm better than most.
Here's how to make the most of it.
Use the position properly
The whole point of Méribel is that you can ski into Courchevel one day and into Val Thorens the next. Most people don't. They stick around the Méribel bowl, which is fine but underuses the lift pass.

Spend a full day in Val Thorens — it's higher, snowier, and the skiing is properly serious. Spend another in Courchevel for the contrast (the pistes are immaculately groomed, the lunches expensive, the people-watching unmatched). Save your Méribel-only days for poor visibility or tired legs; the home bowl is sheltered and easier to navigate when it's snowing hard.
The link via Mont Vallon is the most beautiful in the Three Valleys and the one to do on a clear day. Get there early before the queues build.
Pistes worth knowing about
The
Pic Bleu
chair accesses some of the best red runs in Méribel — empty most mornings because it's slightly off the main flow. The
Mont du Vallon
drop is dramatic and stays in good condition late into the season.
For genuinely quiet skiing, the
St Martin de Belleville
side (over the back of Méribel) is consistently overlooked. The pistes are cruisy, the village is gorgeous, and
La Bouitte
(two Michelin stars) is there for the once-in-a-lifetime lunch if budget allows.
Lunch — where actual skiers eat
La Ferme
on the way to Mottaret is the local classic. Family-run, real Savoyard food, reservations essential in peak weeks.
Les Pierres Plates
at the top of the Saulire lift has the views and reliably good food without the silly prices of the Courchevel side.
For a proper experience,
La Bouitte
in St Marcel (just below St Martin) is worth the trek and the wallet if you want to do one extraordinary lunch. Book weeks ahead.
In Méribel itself,
L'Arpasson
is the picturesque on-piste lunch (don't miss the ride down on the toboggan).
Le Refuge
in Méribel-Village does excellent fondue at sensible prices.
Après and evenings
La Folie Douce
at the top of Saulire is what it is — loud, expensive, on-mountain dancing in ski boots. Go once, have the experience.
Le Rond Point
at the bottom of the home run is the British après institution. Loud, fun, busy from 4pm.
For something more grown-up, the bar at
Le Grand Coeur
is quiet and proper.
Jack's
does decent cocktails. And in Méribel-Village,
Lodge du Village
is the relaxed local-feeling option.
Non-skiing days
The Olympic ice rink (Méribel hosted ice hockey in 1992) is open to the public and properly fun.
Paragliding
off Tougnete on a clear day is unforgettable. And the
Méribel cinema
screens films in English, which sounds boring until you're three days into a snowstorm.
The honest take

Méribel isn't cheap. The food is dearer than Morzine, the lessons cost more than Les Gets, and a week here adds up. What you're paying for is access — to the best linked ski area in the world, with a village that's pleasant rather than purpose-built ugly. For most people, once a year, that's worth it.

title: The Best Things to Do in Verbier (And What Most Visitors Get Wrong)
excerpt: Verbier is one of the great freeride resorts, but you don't need to be a pro to get the best out of it. A local guide to pistes, lunches, and the village beyond the obvious.

seo.title: Best Things to Do in Verbier | Insider Guide to the Swiss Alps
seo.description: What to do in Verbier — runs worth your time, restaurants locals use, and why this Swiss resort rewards visitors who know where to look.

children.text: Verbier divides opinion. To freeriders, it's hallowed ground — the off-piste capital of Europe, home to the Xtreme finals, a place where the lift system feels almost incidental to what the mountain actually offers. To everyone else, it can feel intimidating, expensive, and a bit smug.
The truth is Verbier rewards people who know how to use it. Here's how.
The skiing — and what you're really paying for
The lift-served terrain in Verbier is decent but not extraordinary. What makes Verbier exceptional is the off-piste: the
Vallon d'Arbi
Mont Gelé
Stairway to Heaven
, the bowls under
Mont Fort
. This is some of the best lift-accessible off-piste in the Alps.

If you're not a confident off-piste skier — and most visitors aren't — hire a guide for at least one day. It transforms the holiday. A good guide takes you to terrain you'd never find alone, in safer conditions than you'd ski alone, and shows you a mountain you'd otherwise miss completely.
For on-piste skiing, the
4 Vallées
linked area gives you genuine variety. Head to
Veysonnaz
for long, fast cruising reds.
Thyon
is quieter and good for less confident skiers. The link is fiddly and weather-dependent, so check before committing to a full day across.
Mont Fort — the obligatory pilgrimage
Take the cable car to the top of
Mont Fort

(3330m) at least once. The 360-degree view takes in the Matterhorn and Mont Blanc on a clear day. The piste down is a genuine black — narrow, steep at the top, and one of those runs that feels like an achievement to have done.
Go early. The queue for the top cable car gets serious by 10am in good weather.
Lunch — Swiss prices, Swiss quality
Be warned: lunch in Verbier costs roughly twice what it does in France. Build it into your budget rather than getting a shock on day one.
Chez Dany
in La Marlenaz is the classic — a working farm restaurant, sleigh ride down in the dark after dinner, properly atmospheric.
Le Namaste
at the top of Savoleyres has the views and reliable Swiss-Italian food.
Le Mouton Noir
in the village does excellent simpler food at relatively saner prices.
For an experience:
La Marmotte
is on the way up to Croix de Coeur. Tiny, family-run, no menu, you eat what they're cooking. Worth the effort of finding.
Après and after-dark
Verbier's après scene is famous and largely centred on the
Farinet
complex — the lounge bar, the after-ski stage, the late club. It's expensive, it's busy, and at peak weeks it's where everyone ends up.
For something quieter:
W Bar
at the W Hotel does serious cocktails in a grown-up setting.
Le Rouge
is the long-running locals' favourite, on the way to the home run, with consistently good music and a proper terrace.
Verbier's nightlife is genuinely among the best in the Alps if you're into that. If you're not, the village is small enough that you can avoid it easily.
Non-skiing things worth doing
The
Verbier 3D Sculpture Park
at the top of the Médran lifts is a free, open-air contemporary art park. Unexpected and brilliant on a sunny day.
Paragliding
from Les Ruinettes is the classic non-ski activity — the take-off is one of the best in Europe.
For families, the
Mini Verbier
play areas and
Moon Park
activities offer non-ski options that actually work for children.
The honest reality

Verbier is expensive — not French Alps expensive, Swiss expensive. A week here costs more than the equivalent week in France, the food is dearer, and the lift pass adds up. You're paying for the mountain, the off-piste access, and a village with genuine character.

If you ski intermediate pistes and never venture off them, you'll have a great week in France for less money. If you want off-piste, freeride terrain, and a village with serious mountain culture, Verbier is worth what it costs.

title: The 2026 Ski Horoscope: What Your Star Sign Says About Your Ski Style
excerpt: A slightly unserious — but unsettlingly accurate — look at what your zodiac sign reveals about how you ski, who you ski with, and where you should go this winter.

seo.title: Ski Horoscope 2026 | What Your Star Sign Says About Your Skiing
seo.description: Find your skiing personality by zodiac sign. Where to ski, who to ski with, and what your star sign reveals about your on-piste behaviour.

children.text: We've taught enough lessons to know one thing with certainty: every group has the same characters in it. The cautious one, the show-off, the one who definitely lied on their booking form about being intermediate, the one already drinking at 11am.

We can't prove this is astrologically determined. But we've spent a long time on the slopes, and we've seen things. So, lightheartedly and with our tongues firmly in cheek, here's your ski horoscope for 2026.
Aries (21 March – 19 April)

You're the one who skis off before the instructor has finished the safety briefing. You consider blue runs an insult. You're going to ski faster than you can technically handle, and you're going to enjoy every minute of it.
Resort:
Val d'Isère — the terrain matches your ambition.
Taurus (20 April – 20 May)

You spent six months researching this trip. You have a spreadsheet. You know exactly which restaurant you're eating at on Wednesday. You're going to have an excellent week because you have prepared for it like a small military operation.
Resort:
Méribel — premium quality, plannable, dependable.
Gemini (21 May – 20 June)

You changed your mind about which group lesson to join three times. You're already chatting to a stranger on the chairlift. You will ski every piste once and master none of them, and you'll have a brilliant time anyway.
Resort:
Three Valleys — too many options is exactly right for you.
Cancer (21 June – 22 July)
You booked the chalet specifically because it had a hot tub. You're the one organising the group dinner. Your idea of a perfect ski day involves two runs, a long lunch, and an afternoon nap.
Resort:
Morzine — cosy, sociable, doesn't push too hard.
Leo (23 July – 22 August)

You bought new ski kit specifically for this trip. You have opinions about your goggles. You will be photographed at the top of every notable peak. You ski better than you think you do, but only marginally.
Resort:
Verbier — finally, a resort that takes itself as seriously as you do.
Virgo (23 August – 22 September)

You've done the YouTube tutorials. You know the technical name for what you're doing wrong. You're frustrated that your parallel turns aren't perfectly symmetrical yet. You will, however, improve faster than anyone else in the group.
Resort:
St Anton — technical terrain rewards your perfectionism.
Libra (23 September – 22 October)

You wanted everyone to agree on the resort, which is why you're still deciding in November. You ski beautifully when relaxed and badly when anxious. You're the diplomat who smooths things over after Aries cuts up Capricorn on the chairlift queue.
Resort:
Les Gets — pretty, balanced, no extremes.
Scorpio (23 October – 21 November)

You're suspiciously good at skiing and won't tell anyone how often you actually go. You disappear off-piste at 10am and come back at 4pm with mysterious tales. You make the rest of the group feel inadequate.
Resort:
La Grave — of course it's La Grave.
Sagittarius (22 November – 21 December)

You're the one suggesting heli-skiing, ski touring, and "have we considered Kazakhstan?" Your ski holiday is really an expedition. You will exhaust everyone you ski with, and you will be entirely unaware of this.
Resort:
Chamonix — the only place that can keep up with you.
Capricorn (22 December – 19 January)

You ski with quiet competence and zero fanfare. You've been going to the same resort for twelve years. You don't see the point in changing what works. You ski better than the show-offs, and you know it.
Resort:
Zermatt — classic, reliable, no need to prove anything.
Aquarius (20 January – 18 February)

You're the one wearing a strange retro one-piece ironically. You found a tiny resort no one's heard of and won't stop talking about it. You'll spend an hour explaining why everyone else is doing skiing wrong.
Resort:
Engelberg — niche enough to satisfy you, big enough to ski seriously.
Pisces (19 February – 20 March)

You're skiing today because someone else booked the trip. You're not entirely sure what level you're at. You will, however, fall in love with the mountains in a profound way and become slightly insufferable about it for the next year.
Resort:
Saas-Fee — beautiful, gentle enough to find your feet, dramatic enough to convert you.

title: How to Choose the Right Ski School for Your Level (Without Wasting a Week)
excerpt: Picking the wrong ski school is the most expensive mistake you can make on a ski holiday. Here's how to get it right, from people who run them.

seo.title: How to Choose the Right Ski School | SkiBooker Expert Guide
seo.description: Group vs private, ESF vs independent, how to read the level descriptions properly — a working instructor's guide to picking the right ski school.

children.text: A ski lesson is the single most leveraged purchase you make on a ski holiday. Get the right one, and you transform your week — and possibly your whole skiing life. Get the wrong one, and you spend five days frustrated, stuck on terrain that's too easy or too hard, with an instructor who isn't right for you.
This isn't bad luck. Most of it is decisions you make at the booking stage. Here's how to get them right.
Be honest about your level
The single biggest reason lessons go wrong is that people book the wrong level. Usually too high.

When a school's website says "advanced intermediate — confident on red runs, beginning to explore black", what they mean is: skis parallel at all speeds, controlled on steep terrain, can handle variable snow without falling apart. If you can do most reds but find them tiring and prefer cruising blues, you're a strong intermediate, not an advanced one.
There's no shame in booking the lower level. There's a lot of pain in booking the higher one and spending the week trying to keep up.
Group vs private — the actual trade-offs
Group lessons

are cheaper, more sociable, and forcing yourself to ski with strangers at a fixed level is genuinely good for your skiing. The downside: you ski at the pace of the slowest person, the instructor's attention is divided, and if the group is poorly matched, the whole week suffers.
Private lessons

cost more per hour but typically deliver dramatically more learning per hour. The instructor focuses entirely on you, adapts to your specific issues, and you ski exactly where suits your level. For nervous skiers, mixed-ability families, or anyone with a specific goal (off-piste, moguls, a particular technique), private is almost always worth it.
The hybrid that works well: a couple of private mornings at the start of the week to fix specific issues, then group lessons or free skiing for the rest.
ESF vs independent — the honest picture
In France, you'll see the
ESF

(École du Ski Français) everywhere — the ones in red jackets. They're the established institution and have huge capacity, which means availability when other schools are full. The quality is consistent but varies hugely by instructor; you take what you're given.

Independent schools (often international, frequently English-speaking) tend to be smaller, more selective in their hiring, and offer more flexibility. You can often request specific instructors, get more tailored lessons, and find people who've been teaching your level for years.
Neither is automatically better. Big-brand reliability vs boutique quality — pick the one that suits how you book.
What actually matters in an instructor
Teaching qualification, not just skiing qualification.
Lots of brilliant skiers are mediocre instructors. Look for full ISIA stamp at minimum, or BASI Level 3/4 for British qualifications.
Experience with your level.
A former World Cup racer is wasted on a nervous beginner. An instructor who's spent ten years specialising in adult beginners is gold.
Language fluency.
"Speaks English" can mean anything from "barely" to "fluently". For technical instruction, you want fluently.
Reviews from skiers like you.
A glowing review from an expert means nothing to a beginner and vice versa.
Red flags to watch for
A school that won't tell you who your instructor will be until you arrive.
"Mixed level" groups that combine beginners and intermediates.
Lessons that move groups together regardless of progression.
Anyone who pressures you to book longer lessons than you asked about.
Vague answers about cancellation policies or weather refunds.
Book early

This is the unglamorous truth: the best instructors in popular resorts are booked solid by October or November for peak weeks (Christmas, half-term, February school holidays). If you're skiing in those weeks, you need to book months ahead.
For off-peak weeks (early December, mid-January, March outside school holidays), you've got more flexibility, but the principle stands: book the school before you book the chalet.
The bottom line
The difference between a great instructor and an average one isn't 10%. It's the difference between a transformative week and a forgettable one. Spend the time getting this right.

title: Off-Piste vs Piste: What Beginners Get Wrong About Resort Choice
excerpt: Most ski resort comparisons miss the thing that actually determines whether you'll enjoy your holiday: matching the terrain to your real level, not your aspirational one.

seo.title: Off-Piste vs Piste Resorts | Choosing the Right Ski Resort for Your Level
seo.description: Why famous freeride resorts are wrong for most skiers, and how to pick a resort that matches the terrain you'll actually use. Honest local guidance.

children.text: Every winter, we watch the same scene play out. A group books Verbier, or Chamonix, or St Anton because they've read it's the best resort in the Alps. They arrive. They look at the terrain. They spend the week stuck on the few groomed pistes, looking nervously at the off-piste fields all around them, wondering why everyone said this was the best skiing.
This is the resort-choice mistake — confusing famous off-piste resorts with universally good resorts. They're not the same thing.
What "best resort" actually means

There's no objectively best ski resort. There are resorts that suit different skiers. A resort that's heaven for an experienced freerider might be miserable for a nervous intermediate. A family-friendly cruising paradise might bore a strong skier senseless.
The honest question isn't "what's the best resort?" — it's "what's the best resort for how I actually ski?"
The famous freeride resorts: who they're really for
Resorts like
Verbier, Chamonix, La Grave, St Anton, Engelberg
built their reputations on off-piste terrain. The lift-served piste skiing in these resorts is often surprisingly limited — and what exists is often steep, narrow, or technical.
These resorts make sense if:
You're a confident off-piste skier with a guide, or
You ski genuinely advanced terrain and want to push yourself, or
You're going for the culture and atmosphere and accept the skiing trade-offs.
They don't make sense if you ski mostly groomed pistes and want variety, easy navigation, and lots of forgiving terrain.
Where strong intermediates actually thrive

The sweet spot for most skiers is what you might call a "linked classic" — large connected ski areas with lots of red and blue terrain, good lift infrastructure, and enough black runs to push yourself when you want to.
The Three Valleys
(Méribel, Courchevel, Val Thorens) is the obvious one — vast, well-groomed, something for everyone.
Espace Killy
(Val d'Isère/Tignes) gives you altitude, snow reliability, and a good mix.
Paradiski
(Les Arcs/La Plagne) is underrated.
Portes du Soleil
(Morzine, Les Gets, Avoriaz) is brilliant for families and intermediates.
These resorts let you ski 30+ kilometres a day on varied terrain at your own level without ever feeling out of your depth.
Where beginners and families thrive

True beginner-friendly resorts have specific characteristics: lots of wide, gentle blue terrain; dedicated learner areas separated from through-pistes; ski-in/ski-out access in the village; and ideally, terrain that's intuitive rather than confusing.
Les Gets, La Tania, La Rosière, Alpe d'Huez, Les Saisies
all fit this profile.
Avoriaz
is excellent for families thanks to its car-free village.
Söll and Söll-Going
in Austria are quietly some of the best beginner resorts in Europe.
What to avoid as a beginner: resorts where the village base is also where the steep terrain is, resorts requiring complex lift navigation, and any resort marketed primarily on off-piste.
How to read piste maps honestly
Resort piste maps are marketing documents. Treat them with appropriate scepticism.
Count the genuine beginner pistes — not "easy blues" but actual greens and very gentle blues. Some "family" resorts have surprisingly few.
Look at where the lifts deposit you. If every lift unloads you onto red runs, that's not actually a beginner resort.
Notice connection routes — some resorts force intermediates to use difficult runs to navigate between areas, even though the terrain itself isn't difficult.
The snobbery problem

There's a status hierarchy in skiing that doesn't serve most skiers. Verbier and Chamonix sound impressive. Les Gets and Söll don't. But Les Gets and Söll might be where you'd actually have the better holiday.

The skiers who have the best holidays are the ones who pick the resort that matches their skiing, not the resort that impresses their friends. Be honest about how you ski, choose accordingly, and you'll be the one with the great week.
The exception

If you're booking lessons with a serious instructor in a freeride resort — for example, a private guide in Verbier or off-piste lessons in Chamonix — the calculation changes. You're using the resort's terrain advantage with the support to access it safely. That's exactly what those resorts are for.
For everyone else, pick the resort that matches the skiing you actually do.

title: The Real Cost of a Ski Holiday in 2026 (And Where to Actually Save)
excerpt: Ski holidays have got more expensive. But not all line items rose equally, and not all savings are smart ones. A working breakdown from people in the industry.

seo.title: Real Cost of a Ski Holiday 2026 | Where to Save Without Compromising
seo.description: What a ski holiday actually costs in 2026, where prices have risen most, and the smart places to save without ruining your week. Honest industry breakdown.

children.text: Ski holidays have got noticeably more expensive over the past few seasons. Lift passes, mountain restaurants, accommodation, transfers — it has all gone up. But the price rises haven't been uniform, and the conventional wisdom about where to save isn't always right.
Here's an honest breakdown of where the money actually goes on a ski holiday, and where you can sensibly cut without ruining the week.
A realistic week's budget
For a couple skiing in a mid-range French resort, mid-season, here's roughly what you're looking at in 2026 (per person, six days skiing):
Flights:
Transfers:
Accommodation (catered chalet or apartment):
Lift pass (6 days):
Equipment hire:
Lessons or guiding:
£0–£400+ (group lessons average £180–£250 for the week; private lessons run higher)
Food and drink:
£350–£700 (the variable one)
Insurance:
That's a realistic range of
£1,640–£3,430 per person
for a week. The spread tells you something important: most of the variation isn't in the unavoidable costs, it's in the choices.
Where prices rose the most
Three categories have seen the steepest increases:
Mountain restaurants
have gone up significantly. A modest lunch on the slopes that was €25 a few years ago is now €40+ in many resorts. Swiss resorts are particularly painful.
Lift passes
in major linked areas have outpaced inflation. The Three Valleys, Paradiski, and Espace Killy passes have all crept up year on year.
Last-minute accommodation
has become noticeably more expensive. The flexibility premium that used to exist has shrunk; booking early now saves you meaningfully more than it used to.
Where to genuinely save
Book early.
This is by far the single biggest lever. Six-month-out chalet bookings often run 20-30% cheaper than three-month-out. Early-bird lift pass deals are real and worth taking.
Eat lunch off-piste.

A packed lunch in your backpack saves €30+ per person per day. Even better: ski down to a village for lunch where prices are half what they are mid-mountain. In Méribel, dropping into Méribel-Village; in Verbier, skiing down to Le Châble; in Morzine, the village itself.
Travel mid-week to mid-week.
Saturday-to-Saturday is the most expensive changeover. Sunday-to-Sunday or Monday-to-Monday can be 15-20% cheaper for flights, transfers, and accommodation — and the lifts are far quieter on Sundays.
Go second week of January or mid-March.

Pre-half-term January and post-Easter March are the genuinely cheap weeks. Snow is usually excellent in January; March is variable but often glorious. Avoid them only if you specifically need school holidays.
Stay in a less famous resort.
Les Gets instead of Méribel, Champagny-en-Vanoise instead of Courchevel, La Tzoumaz instead of Verbier — same lift area, dramatically lower cost.
Where not to save
Don't skimp on lessons.

This is the easiest place to think you can save and the worst place to actually save. A poorly-matched group lesson at half price isn't a saving, it's a wasted week. Pay for the right lesson with the right instructor.
Don't cheap out on boots.
Rented boots that don't fit will ruin your week faster than anything else. If the rental shop has fitted you something painful, go back and demand a swap, or pay extra for premium-fit rentals.
Don't skip insurance.
A serious skiing injury without insurance is financially ruinous. The £50–£80 for a winter-sports policy is non-negotiable.
Don't drive 10 hours to save £100.
Tired drivers in bad weather end up in ditches. The savings versus flying-plus-transfer rarely justify the time and risk unless you're going for a fortnight or have lots of kit.
The thing that saves you the most money
It's boring, and it's this: book early, in a less famous resort, mid-week to mid-week, in a non-school-holiday week, with lessons matched to your actual level.
Do those five things and you'll spend half what someone going to Méribel half-term will spend, and you'll probably have a better week.
The reality check

A good ski holiday isn't cheap. But "good" doesn't require Méribel-in-half-term prices. We've taught families having brilliant weeks in Les Gets on tight budgets, and miserable weeks in Verbier on huge ones. Where you spend matters more than how much you spend.

title: Why You Should Book Ski Lessons in Advance (From a Working Instructor)
excerpt: By the time you book your chalet, the best instructors are already gone. Here's why ski lessons are the one thing you should book before everything else.

seo.title: Why Book Ski Lessons in Advance | Insider Booking Advice
seo.description: A working ski instructor explains why early lesson booking matters more than people realise — availability, instructor quality, and the cost of leaving it late.

children.text: Every January, we have the same conversation about a hundred times. Someone walks into the ski school office on the Saturday afternoon they arrive, asks about lessons starting Monday, and looks crestfallen when they're told the only available slots are 8am, with whichever instructor happens to be free.

The good lessons in good resorts in peak weeks are booked out by October. This isn't a marketing line — it's an operational reality, and most visitors don't understand it until they've been caught out by it.
Here's why advance booking matters more than most people realise.
The instructor pool is finite

A ski resort has a fixed number of qualified instructors. There's no surge capacity — when half-term hits and demand triples, the same instructors are working the same hours. The difference is just which ones get booked first.

In a typical mid-sized resort, the highly-rated, fluent-English-speaking, full-ISIA-qualified instructors number in the dozens, not hundreds. In peak weeks, they're booked solid. The people booking in November get them. The people booking in January don't.
What "fully booked" actually means

When a ski school tells you they're "fully booked" in February half-term, what they often mean is: they're fully booked with their best instructors. They can probably still take you, but you'll be allocated to whoever's available — which might be a trainee, a newly-qualified instructor, or someone covering outside their usual age group or level.

This isn't dishonest. They genuinely have capacity. But the gap between "the best instructor in the school" and "whoever's spare on Tuesday morning" is enormous, and you don't know which one you're getting if you book late.
Early bookers get to request specific instructors by name. Late bookers take what they're given.
Group lessons fill predictably

Group lessons in particular operate on tight capacity. A typical group is 6-8 people. Once a group is full, that's it — they can't squeeze in a ninth person without ruining the lesson for the existing eight.

Popular levels (low intermediate, high beginner) fill first because that's where most skiers cluster. By the time you're booking three weeks out for half-term, "Level 3 — comfortable on blue runs" is gone in every school in the resort. You're either being put into Level 2 (too easy) or Level 4 (too hard) or skipping group lessons entirely.
Private lessons fill even faster

Private one-to-one lessons with named, requested instructors are the first thing to disappear from booking calendars. Some long-standing instructors are booked 18 months out by repeat clients who return every year.

If you want a specific instructor — particularly one recommended to you, or one you've used before — book them as soon as you've decided your dates. Even before you've booked flights. Instructors will hold dates against deposits well in advance.
The off-peak exception

If you're booking for a non-school-holiday week — early December, mid-January (after the first week), early February (before half-term), mid-March — the urgency is lower. Two or three months ahead is usually fine.
For Christmas/New Year, February half-term, and Easter, you should be booking by September or October.
What to book first
The order most people get wrong: 1. Flights 2. Accommodation 3. Lift passes 4. Lessons 5. Transfers
The order that actually works better: 1.
Lessons
(locks in the best instructor and shapes your week) 2.
Accommodation
(now you can match location to where lessons start) 3.
Flights
(now you know your transfer day requirements) 4.
Transfers and lift passes
(admin items that book late just fine)
This sounds inverted but it's right. Lessons are the most capacity-constrained item with the biggest quality variance. Lock them in first. Everything else has more flexibility.
The smart move

If you know roughly when you're skiing — even if not the exact week — contact ski schools early and ask about their booking patterns. A good school will tell you honestly: "Christmas is filling up, half-term has limited availability, we have flexibility in March." That information is gold for planning.

Many schools also offer flexible booking — you reserve an instructor's time with a deposit, and the exact lesson types can be confirmed closer to the date. This is the way to lock in quality without committing every detail months out.
The bottom line

Ski lessons aren't like restaurant reservations where you can usually walk in and find something acceptable. They're more like seats at a specific concert: when they're gone, they're gone, and the alternative options are meaningfully worse. Book early, get the right instructor, and the rest of the holiday builds itself around a good foundation.
